subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]
passage: Darshan Mama leaned back in his chair. "Madhav, when I went to the engineering hostel in Chennai, I was the only one from our hill district. The first month everyone stared at my woollen cap, even in that heat. People asked, 'Do all of you eat that? Do all of you talk like that?' I felt I had to be perfect, because if I failed an exam, they'd say hill boys can't do engineering. I was carrying the whole district on my back. What changed it was Selvam, the boy in the next room. He never asked about 'my people.' He asked what music I liked, and whether I wanted to join the chess club. Slowly I became Darshan who plays chess badly, not the hill boy. So when someone new joins your office, ask about them, not only about where they're from."

Usha, the shift supervisor, set aside dates and water for him and asked nothing about religion. Instead she asked about the cricket team he played for on Sundays. He talked for twenty minutes. Someone laughed at his story about a lost ball. For once, nobody asked what his people thought. He was just Imran, who bowls leg-spin.

qa.a: She quietly set aside dates and water and asked about his cricket, meeting his needs without making him explain his religion again.

subtype: Being the only one from your group [Receiver]
passage: In the Kolkata college hostel, Suraj was the only student from Tamil Nadu, and he felt it at every meal. People watched him eat rice with his fingers. Someone asked if he'd brought "the spicy stuff all of you eat." When a professor asked, "What do people down south think about this?", every head turned to him, and he answered stiffly, as if he were a whole state. His roommate Wasim never did that. Wasim asked what Suraj himself thought about films, football, the terrible canteen tea. One night Wasim dragged him to the quiz club, where Suraj answered a question on old radio sets that nobody else knew. At breakfast the next morning someone said, "Oh, you're the radio guy." Suraj laughed. It was the first time he'd been known for something that was only his.

qa.q: Which club did Wasim drag Suraj to?
qa.a: The quiz club.

qa.q: Why did Suraj answer the professor stiffly?
qa.a: With every head turning to him, he felt forced to speak for a whole state rather than as himself, which made him tense.

qa.q: What choice did Wasim make that helped Suraj be seen as himself?
qa.a: Wasim asked about Suraj's own views and took him to the quiz club, where Suraj could show his own interests.

qa.q: What might the student who said 'you're the radio guy' now notice about Suraj?
qa.a: That student now sees Suraj as a person with his own knowledge, not as a sample of people from the south.

grounding: A student who is the only one from his state in a hostel feels watched and made to represent everyone, until a roommate's contact lets him be an individual.

"Dolma, you're from Ladakh, na? Is it true you all drink butter tea the whole day?"
"Some of us. I prefer coffee."
"Do all Ladakhis..."
"Rakesh, I can only tell you about me."
Rakesh laughed and wandered off. Dolma turned back to her circuit diagram, jaw tight.
Uday, who shared her lab table, pulled up his chair. "That's the third time today, isn't it?"
"Fourth. The warden wants me to say something about my culture at Freshers' Night. As if I'm a brochure."
"Do you want to?"
"No. I want to talk about the robot arm."
"Then talk about the robot arm. I'll tell the warden you're busy with the tech fest." Uday leaned over the diagram. "Why did you put the motor there?"
For twenty minutes Dolma explained torque and forgot to feel watched.

qa.q: What did the warden want Dolma to do at Freshers' Night?
qa.a: To say something about her culture.

qa.q: What does Dolma's tight jaw after Rakesh's question suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she was tired and irritated at being treated as an example of her whole region rather than as herself.

qa.q: What did Uday do that let Dolma be an individual?
qa.a: He asked what she wanted, offered to handle the warden, and asked about her robot arm, treating her as a fellow engineer.

qa.q: How might Rakesh see his questions compared with how they felt to Dolma?
qa.a: Rakesh probably thinks the questions are just curiosity, not realising the repeated questions make Dolma carry a whole region on her shoulders.

grounding: The only student from her region in a hostel feels curious eyes and pressure to represent everyone, until a classmate treats her as an individual.

passage:
I'm Mehak, and last year I was the only trainee from Punjab in a batch of forty at a textile firm in Coimbatore. In the first month someone asked me to do a little dance at every team lunch. When there was news from Punjab, people turned to me as if I were the spokesperson. I started choosing my words as if a whole state were being graded on them. It was exhausting, and a little lonely.
Things shifted because of Uday, from the dyeing unit. On a slow afternoon he asked what I did at weekends. I told him I watch birds at the lake. He came along the next Sunday with borrowed binoculars and asked a hundred questions about kingfishers, none about Punjab.
After that the team started calling me the bird person. I've never liked a nickname more. It was mine, not my state's.

qa.q: What does Mehak do at weekends?
qa.a: Mehak watches birds at the lake.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel being treated like a spokesperson for Punjab?
qa.a: Mehak felt exhausted and a little lonely, choosing every word as if a whole state were being graded.

qa.q: What did Uday's weekend question change?
qa.a: It let Mehak be seen through a personal interest, birdwatching, instead of as an example of a region, and the team followed.

qa.q: Why might Uday have asked about weekends rather than about Punjab?
qa.a: Uday seems to have been curious about Mehak as a person, perhaps sensing the weight of all the other questions.

grounding: The only trainee from one state feels watched and pressed to represent everyone, until a colleague's interest lets them be an individual.
